extracted.intended_audience: credit card issuers, compliance officers, regulated entities, and rulemaking stakeholders (legal/regulatory community)
extracted.subtask_description: Rationale and analytical criteria the CFPB used to set, repeal, and replace the late-fee safe harbor threshold for Larger Card Issuers under TILA (CARD Act). Covers statutory interpretation, data sources, cost measurement, deterrence, and implementation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable and proportional standard (TILA section 149(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The safe harbor amount must be an amount that is presumed to be reasonable and proportional to the omission or violation to which the fee or charge relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB analyzed whether a threshold is a reasonable proxy for the statutory definition of “reasonable and proportional” such that any fee under the threshold should be presumed to have met that standard. The safe harbor is intended to be a presumptive compliance mechanism, not an unconditional license to charge any fee under the threshold if inconsistent with the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pre-charge-off collection costs as the relevant 'costs' for setting late fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs for purposes of the cost analysis provisions in §1026.52(b)(1)(i) for determining penalty fee amounts include costs associated with collection of late payments and exclude losses and associated costs (including holding reserves and funding delinquent accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB explicitly clarifies that post-charge-off collection costs are not included. CFPB estimated pre-charge-off collection costs as a percentage (75% in initial analysis, 80% in updated analysis) of total collection costs reported in Y-14 data and used these estimates to determine safe harbor amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on average Larger Card Issuer pre-charge-off collection costs to set safe harbor for Larger Card Issuers
rubrics_metrics.description: In implementing the safe harbor for Larger Card Issuers, the CFPB primarily focused on whether a particular safe harbor amount would cover the pre-charge-off collection costs of the average Larger Card Issuer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach allows average Larger Card Issuers to rely on the safe harbor without conducting issuer-specific cost analyses while avoiding setting the safe harbor so high that it exceeds costs for most issuers. CFPB used Y-14 and Y-14+ data and issuer surveys to estimate the average pre-charge-off cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor is discretionary and need not exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a safe harbor is an exercise of discretionary rulemaking authority; the CFPB is not statutorily required to set a safe harbor amount and may choose not to provide one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB notes that a safe harbor may be repealed and that the decision to repeal or set a specific amount is independent and severable from other parts of a regulation. Without a safe harbor, issuers can rely on the cost analysis provisions to ensure compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor must not be set so high that it enables fees contrary to statute
rubrics_metrics.description: A discretionary safe harbor should not be so high that it allows fees that are not reasonable and proportional and therefore inconsistent with the CARD Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB criticized the Board's prior analysis for failing to consider whether the safe harbor could be too high (i.e., permit issuers to recover fees that exceed reasonable and proportional amounts). This is an independent rationale for lowering or repealing overly high safe harbor thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical data sources (Y-14, Y-14+, card agreement surveys, information orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB relied on available data including Y-14 reporting, Y-14+ specialized issuer data, quarterly card agreement submissions, and information obtained via information orders to analyze late fee income and collection costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB used these datasets to calculate fee-income-to-cost ratios, examine disclosed maximum late fees, and assess average late fees. CFPB emphasizes that such data were not available when the Board originally set the safe harbor in 2010.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare monthly late fee income to estimated pre-charge-off collection costs with a 2–6 month lag to account for timing
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing monthly data, CFPB compared each month's late fee income for a particular portfolio to the portfolio's average estimated pre-charge-off collection costs that occurred two through six months later to account for lag between assessment of fees and incurrence of collection costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method addresses seasonality and delay between when a late fee was assessed and when substantial collection costs are incurred. CFPB developed monthly estimates of income-to-cost ratios for 2013–September 2022 using this lagged comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for seasonality and anomalous periods (e.g., pandemic months) in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Late payments and late-fee income exhibit seasonal patterns and pandemic-era anomalies; analyses should consider these effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB notes pandemic months (April–June 2020 and Feb–May 2021) where late-fee income was reduced relative to subsequent collection costs. CFPB weighted averages across issuers and market segments and examined stability since early 2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative, transparent calculation choices (use highest-market fee and division heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB used conservative assumptions in deriving the $8 fee — dividing $41 (the highest late fee charged in the market) by five and rounding to the nearest dollar — and discussed alternative bases that would yield even lower safe harbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using $41 and a one-fifth (20%) reduction was a cautious approach; CFPB noted a less conservative base (e.g., $30 or $31) would imply a $6 safe harbor. CFPB also tested sensitivity to using 75% vs. 80% pre-charge-off cost assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give primary weight to costs over deterrence and consumer conduct when setting precise safe harbor amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if required to consider costs, deterrence, and consumer conduct, CFPB determined that costs deserve the most weight because they are most closely correlated to issuer consequences of late payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deterrence and consumer conduct are considered but are harder to quantify and have a more tenuous link to fee amounts. CFPB used deterrence/consumer conduct to corroborate, not to override, cost-based determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider deterrence and consumer conduct as corroborating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Deterrence and consumer conduct inform whether the safe harbor amount will still discourage late payments and reflect consumer behavior, but should not dominate the cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB analyzed whether an $8 fee would have a deterrent effect (e.g., comparing fee to minimum payments and computing effective APRs), noted other issuer tools to deter late payments (credit-line decreases, reward limits, penalty rates, autopay, notifications), and recognized uncertainty in predicting behavioral responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate deterrence via comparison to minimum payment and effective APRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess deterrent effect by comparing the safe harbor fee to typical minimum payments and calculating implied effective APRs for delayed payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB example: for a $100 minimum payment made one month late, an $8 late fee implies an effective APR of 96%; for borrowing $40 for 10 days and paying $8 late fee implies ~730% APR. Such comparisons support that even $8 can be a powerful deterrent for attentive consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider issuer benefits from safe harbor (compliance certainty, administrative simplicity, reduced litigation risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: The safe harbor provides issuers benefits (compliance certainty, administrative simplicity, reduced litigation risk) that should be considered when choosing an amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB explicitly weighed these issuer benefits alongside cost coverage and found $8 would cover average pre-charge-off costs while providing these benefits for Larger Card Issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit issuers with above-average costs to use cost analysis provisions instead of safe harbor
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the safe harbor is discretionary, issuers whose pre-charge-off collection costs exceed the safe harbor amount may opt to determine a late fee using the individualized cost analysis provisions in §1026.52(b)(1)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB estimated a small number of issuers/portfolios might not recover pre-charge-off costs at $8; those issuers can choose the cost analysis method, reduce collection costs, or recover costs via rates/other charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply safe harbor to Larger Card Issuers based on scale and expected cost structures even when direct data are unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB applies the $8 safe harbor to certain issuers for which it lacks total collections and late-fee revenue data because those issuers (and affiliates) have at least one million open credit card accounts and are expected to have similar economies of scale and pre-charge-off cost structures as Y-14+ issuers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB used expertise and market research to assume similar mechanisms for efficient collection and lower per-incident costs than Smaller Card Issuers; these issuers are also likely to have resources for cost analysis if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude state/local/international policy evidence and pre-CARD Act issuer fee baselines as determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of state, local, or international approaches or pre-CARD Act issuer-set fees reflects policy decisions that are not determinative of whether a safe harbor appropriately meets CARD Act standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB concluded thresholds should be set based on the cost-analysis provisions and cost data, noting there is no legislative history justification for assuming Congress intended only to curtail further increases rather than lower fees from pre-existing baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize safe harbor will not cover all issuers/portfolios and acknowledge tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: The CARD Act does not require a safe harbor that covers costs for all issuers or the entire costs of every omission; CFPB accepts that some issuers/portfolios may not recover full costs under the safe harbor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB estimated fewer than four (or under six in updated analysis) of the sampled issuers had pre-charge-off costs significantly above one-fifth of fee income; for such portfolios, issuing-specific cost analyses may be more appropriate and safe harbor remains optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using external cost estimates (e.g., trade association data), ensure alignment with permitted cost categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost data for delinquent accounts (e.g., 60+ days late) may include items not permitted under §1026.52(b)(1)(i) and may not represent average pre-charge-off costs across all late-payment incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB rejected some trade-association figures as less relevant because they covered a subset (60+ days) and included post-charge-off or loss-related costs excluded from permitted cost calculations; importance of knowing facts/circumstances underlying attributable expenses was noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple robustness checks and updated data to confirm conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB supplemented initial analysis with additional months of Y-14 data, updated post-charge-off commission rate estimates (moving pre-charge-off percentage from 75% to 80%), and confidential data from specialized issuers to test whether $8 would cover average pre-charge-off costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB presented figures (e.g., fee-income-to-cost ratios above five or six for recent months) and alternative calculations (quarter-over-quarter ratios) to show consistency of conclusions under different assumptions and data additions.
